# Irrigation policy — bed 3

## Thresholds

| Soil moisture | Action |
|---|---|
| Above 50 per cent | Suspend irrigation. Running the system here risks waterlogging and root rot. |
| 30 to 50 per cent | Normal range. Run the standard schedule. |
| 20 to 30 per cent | Dry. Increase to twice daily if air temperature exceeds 30 degrees. |
| Below 20 per cent | Deficit. Run a manual cycle the same day and investigate the cause. |
| Below 12 per cent | Critical. Treat as a fault, not a weather event. Inspect filter, emitters and controller schedule before adding water. |

Critical. Treat as a fault, not a weather event. Inspect filter, emitters and controller schedule before adding water. | ## Why the critical threshold is a fault, not a dry spell

Evapotranspiration alone will not take a correctly irrigated bed below about 18 per cent in this climate. A reading under 12 per cent means water is not reaching the roots, and adding more water through a blocked line achieves nothing. The September 2026 decline to 11 per cent was a controller schedule that had silently reverted after a firmware update, and three days were lost to the assumption that it was simply hot.

## Standard schedule

## Standard schedule Once daily at 06:00 for 12 minutes. Morning irrigation is preferred: evening watering leaves foliage wet overnight and encourages fungal disease, and midday watering loses a substantial fraction to evaporation before it reaches the root zone.

## Hot-weather schedule

When air temperature exceeds 30 degrees on two consecutive days, move to twice daily at 06:00 and 18:00, 10 minutes each. Do not simply lengthen the morning cycle; beyond about 15 minutes the bed cannot absorb water as fast as it is delivered and the excess runs off.

e morning cycle; beyond about 15 minutes the bed cannot absorb water as fast as it is delivered and the excess runs off. Return to the standard schedule once temperature has been below 30 degrees for two consecutive days.

## After rainfall

Suspend irrigation while soil moisture remains above 50 per cent. Resume at the standard schedule when it falls back into the normal range. Do not resume on a fixed number of days after rain — resume on the reading.

sume on a fixed number of days after rain — resume on the reading.

## Alerting

Three conditions should raise an alert: 1. Soil moisture below 20 per cent at any reading.
2. A decline with no sawtooth for more than three consecutive days, which indicates irrigation is not reaching the bed even though moisture is still within range.
3. Any reading above 95 per cent, which usually means water has entered the probe cable rather than that the bed is flooded.

Condition 2 is the one most often missing from a monitoring setup, and it is the one that would have caught the September filter blockage on the third day rather than the ninth.

# Maintenance log — bed 3 sensor station, September 2026

## 2026-09-01 — Season start

Station brought back into service. Probe A calibrated: dry reference 4 per cent, wet reference 91 per cent. Within tolerance. Temperature and humidity sensor replaced with a new unit after last season's failure. Light sensor cleaned.

Irrigation controller set to run 06:00 daily for 12 minutes.

## 2026-09-09 — Irrigation failure

Light sensor cleaned.

Irrigation controller set to run 06:00 daily for 12 minutes.

## 2026-09-09 — Irrigation failure Soil moisture had declined steadily from 42 per cent on the 1st to 19 per cent by the 9th with no sawtooth, indicating the daily irrigation had not been reaching the bed. Found the inline filter blocked with grit. Cleaned filter and ran a manual 20-minute cycle on the evening of the 9th.

Note for next season: a flat decline over more than four days should trigger an alert. We lost eight days before anyone looked at the graph.

## 2026-09-10 — Recovery confirmed Moisture recovered to 46 per cent after the manual cycle, consistent with the wet reference, so the probe itself is sound. Automatic schedule resumed.

## 2026-09-19 — Heat event

Air temperature reached 33.1 degrees, the highest so far this season, rising to 34.2 on the 20th. Soil moisture fell faster than the usual decline, reaching 20 per cent by the 20th despite irrigation running normally. This is evapotranspiration, not a fault.

Increased irrigation to twice daily, 06:00 and 18:00, for the duration of the heat.

## 2026-09-24 — Second decline investigated Moisture reached 11 per cent on the 24th, the lowest reading of the month. Initially suspected a second filter blockage. Inspection found the filter clear and the emitters flowing. Cause was the twice-daily schedule having been reverted to once daily on the 22nd by a controller firmware update that reset the schedule to defaults.

Schedule restored on the evening of the 24th. Firmware auto-update disabled.

## 2026-09-26 — Rain Natural rainfall over the 25th to 27th brought moisture to 58 per cent, the highest of the month. Irrigation suspended for three days. Light readings fell to 5,200 lux on the 27th, consistent with heavy overcast.

## Outstanding actions

- Fit a pressure switch downstream of the filter so a blockage raises an alert rather than waiting for the moisture graph to be noticed.
- Probe A due for recalibration at the start of the next season.
- Replace the cable on probe B; sheath is cracked where it leaves the conduit.

# Soil moisture probe — field guide

## What the probe measures

The capacitive probe reports a percentage derived from the dielectric constant of the surrounding soil. It does not measure water volume directly. Two soils at the same true water content can read several percentage points apart if their mineral composition differs, so a reading is only comparable against other readings from the same probe in the same bed.

## Calibration

Calibrate in two points before the first deployment of a season.

s from the same probe in the same bed.

## Calibration

Calibrate in two points before the first deployment of a season. 1. Hold the probe in still air, away from your hand, and record the reading. This is the dry reference. On a healthy probe it falls between 2 and 6 per cent.
2. Submerge the probe to the marked line in tap water and record the reading. This is the wet reference, normally between 88 and 96 per cent.

If the dry reference exceeds 10 per cent the probe body has absorbed moisture and must be dried for 24 hours before reuse. If the wet reference falls below 80 per cent, the sensing element has degraded and the probe should be replaced.

Recalibrate after any of the following: a new season, a probe that has been submerged past the marked line, or a reading that disagrees with a neighbouring probe by more than 8 percentage points.

## Installation depth

Install at root depth for the crop in question, not at the surface. For leafy vegetables this is 100 to 150 mm; for tomatoes and peppers, 200 to 300 mm. A probe installed too shallow tracks the weather rather than the plant, and will show a sharp spike after every light shower that never reaches the roots.

ks the weather rather than the plant, and will show a sharp spike after every light shower that never reaches the roots. Backfill firmly. An air gap along the probe body is the single most common cause of readings that are implausibly low and unusually stable.

## Known failure modes

**Saline soil.** Dissolved salts raise the apparent dielectric constant, so a saline bed reads wetter than it is. Readings drift upward over a season as fertiliser salts accumulate. Flush the bed or relocate the probe.

**Direct sun on the cable.** UV degradation of the cable sheath admits moisture to the conductors, producing intermittent spikes to 99 per cent. Route cable under mulch.

e cable sheath admits moisture to the conductors, producing intermittent spikes to 99 per cent. Route cable under mulch. **Freezing.** Below 0 degrees the water in the soil changes phase and the probe reads near-dry regardless of actual content. Readings taken below 2 degrees should be discarded, not corrected.

## Expected daily pattern

A correctly installed probe in an irrigated bed shows a sawtooth: a sharp rise within fifteen minutes of irrigation, then a slow decline of 2 to 5 percentage points per day depending on temperature and canopy cover. A flat line over several days means either no irrigation has occurred or the probe has lost soil contact.
